synopsis: Latency is a first-order stopping-distance contributor: at 5–15 km/h it can account for half or more of the distance, motivating a calibrated point-mass model with measured latency, brake build-up lag and worst-case deceleration dependent on grade, payload and surface [f144, f146]. ISO 21815-3:2023 frames collision-avoidance distance around detection, decision and action time, machine stopping distance and a safety distance; inadequate detection range in dust requires slower driving or prevents a promise to stop [f6680, f11330]. Real-machine and proving-ground tests are recommended as anchors for actual stopping behaviour, while validation should cover the full causal timing chain rather than minimum stopping distance alone [f551, f5345, f7786]. Published validation of simulated heavy-machine braking on gravel, mud, ice or slopes was not found, nor was an off-road automatic-braking stopping-distance tolerance; the broader terramechanics review also found no adequate validation across 100+ site types, but did not review Project Chrono validation literature [f253, f7808, f10611]. Coverage and acceptance remain limited: the reported mining stopping tests covered only unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, South Africa's Regulation 8.10 specifies no fixed stopping-distance test, and ISO's example stopping calculations are not a validation method [f5182, f2281, f7729].
